title: Supervised Contextual Post-Classification Method for Geospatial Objects
author: Ferrara, Lindberg, et al.

steps.title: Acquire georeferenced input raster
steps.instruction: Obtain a georeferenced raster image of the study area; for the example use a 2013 RGB orthophoto with 25 cm pixel resolution, scale 1:10 000, covering approximately 21 km² (source: Regione Siciliana, Assessorato Regionale Territorio e Ambiente, Dipartimento di Urbanistica, Area 2 Interdipartimentale, “Elemento di proprietà della Regione Siciliana ceduto in data 31/01/2023 al n. 2023‑S‑3466”).

steps.title: Define conceptual spaces
steps.instruction: Specify the semantic objects to extract from the image as “conceptual spaces”. In the case study define three spaces: (1) Orchard of century‑old olive trees, (2) Mediterranean garden, (3) Modern olive plantation. Describe each space by its characteristic spatial configuration and associated elements (e.g., tree density, presence of other vegetation, row planting, soil tiling, etc.).

steps.title: Create training area polygons
steps.instruction: In QGIS, draw a polygon (saved as a shapefile) that exactly delimits each conceptual space on the input raster. Produce three training‑area shapefiles, one for each of the three conceptual spaces defined above; these polygons will be used in the training and post‑classification steps.

steps.title: Pre‑classify image with K‑means
steps.instruction: Run an unsupervised K‑means classification on the input raster using Orfeo Toolbox (OTB). Reduce the image to 30 spectral classes (any number of classes is allowed, but larger numbers increase computational load and do not necessarily improve thematic precision).

steps.title: Compute feature vectors & criteria
steps.instruction: For each pixel inside each training‑area polygon, calculate a 30‑dimensional contextual feature vector containing the Euclidean nearest‑neighbour distance from the pixel to the nearest pixel of every spectral class obtained in Step 4. Then, for each spectral class, determine the largest nearest‑neighbour distance among all pixels of that class within the training area (the spatial‑contextual criterion).

substeps.instruction: Calculate contextual feature vectors (30‑dimensional Euclidean distances).
Determine the largest nearest‑neighbour distance for each class (spatial‑contextual criterion).

steps.title: Perform supervised contextual post‑classification
steps.instruction: Using CS.py, re‑classify every pixel of the whole pre‑classified image. For each pixel, compare its contextual feature vector to the spatial‑contextual criteria derived in Step 5: if the pixel’s nearest‑neighbour distance to a class exceeds the largest distance recorded for that class in the training area, assign it to class 0 (different context); otherwise assign it to class 1 (same context). Repeat the procedure for each training area to obtain separate binary rasters for each conceptual space.

substeps.instruction: Re‑classify pixels pixel‑by‑pixel based on the criteria.
Assign class 1 to pixels matching the training‑area context, class 0 otherwise.
Run the process separately for each of the three training areas.

steps.title: Post‑process binary output image
steps.instruction: The result of Step 6 is a binary raster (0/1). Optional post‑processing includes vectorising the raster, adjusting symbology, and exporting for further analysis. Note that CS.py uses ~4 bytes per pixel for feature vectors, 1 byte for spatial‑contextual criteria, and 1 byte for the final classification (e.g., a 10 × 10 pixel image requires ~600 bytes of RAM). Install CS.py as a zip package within QGIS before running the workflow.

substeps.instruction: Vectorise the binary raster if needed.
Modify symbology for visualisation or analysis.
Be aware of RAM usage: 4 B/pixel (features) + 1 B/pixel (criteria) + 1 B/pixel (classification).

description: In recent work [17], we have shown how unsupervised contextual and spatial-relational analysis can be applied to extract from a single image of the Earth useful classes carrying information that, integrated with other sources of evidence (e.g. local ecological knowledge, ground truth), allows reading the multiple layers of meanings in the historical, cultural and ecological formation processes of a heterogeneous landscape. The method we present here is the supervised version of the same geospatial approach. In our method, a conceptual space such as, for instance, “intensive orchard of crop x” is categorised in terms of context, meaning with this word the peculiar spatial configurations of a conceptual space as defined by the contextual relationships among its constitutive elements in terms of biophysical features, human-nature processes, intentionalities and ecological dynamics. In our method, these contexts are then computed as training areas, whose information will be then used to set the clustering conditions of a supervised classification of the entire image data. From a computational point of view, our method is operationalised by CONTEXTS.py (CS.py), a plugin for the Open-Source GIS (Geographical Information System) program QGIS, written in Python programming language. With CS.py, it is possible to use training areas, created by the user at diverse and multiple scales, to identify and extract in the image data conceptual spaces whose spatial contexts have the same spatial features present in the training areas. The overall supervised contextual post-classification procedure automated by CS.py consists of two analytical steps: 1) Training phase and 2) Contextual post-classification, detailed below together with a description of the four preliminary steps needed to prepare the input image and training areas for the analysis, as well as post-processing stage (Fig. 1):Step 1 (Preliminary): Input image acquisitionStep 2 (Preliminary): Conceptual spaces definitionSt
